issues.legal_issue: A government’s grant of general relief to a class of persons before an election, and political statements promoting or explaining that relief, do not establish a corrupt practice where the relief is not a gratification and the government actors are not shown to have acted as the candidate’s agents.
material_facts: A state government enacted an ordinance exempting certain small agricultural holdings from land revenue after the issue had been debated and advocated by different political parties.
The relief applied to a large number of agriculturists and was granted by the government through the ordinance, not by the political party supporting the candidate.
The chief minister announced the relief and a party member circulated a pamphlet supporting the party’s electoral position on the issue.
The evidence did not establish that the chief minister or the pamphlet’s author acted as the candidate’s agent.
issues.conclusion: The charge of corrupt practice under section 123(1)(A) was not established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 123(1)(A) concerns a candidate’s or agent’s gift, offer, or promise of gratification to induce electoral support. General relief granted by the government through an ordinance was not such gratification, and the government’s political alignment with the candidate’s party did not make the government the candidate’s agent. The chief minister’s announcement and the party member’s pamphlet did not establish agency. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: election_petition_challenging_election and government_enacts_general_public_relief and relief_is_not_candidate_gratification and (government_not_candidate_agent and public_speakers_not_candidate_agents)

predicates.election_petition_challenging_election: A petitioner seeks to set aside an election by alleging a corrupt practice.
predicates.government_enacts_general_public_relief: The government grants relief to a class of people through a general governmental measure.
predicates.relief_is_not_candidate_gratification: The relief is granted as a governmental measure rather than as a gift, offer, or promise of gratification by or for the candidate.
predicates.government_not_candidate_agent: The evidence does not show that the government acted as the candidate’s agent in granting the relief.
predicates.public_speakers_not_candidate_agents: The evidence does not show that the officials or political speakers who announced or promoted the relief acted as the candidate’s agents.

issues.definition: When an election challenge concerns general relief granted by government, and neither the relief nor the conduct of those announcing it is attributable to the candidate as gratification or agency, the corrupt-practice charge is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A government’s announcement of increased employee allowances to meet an employment demand does not establish a corrupt practice where the government’s action is not shown to be gratification provided by or through the candidate or to have been undertaken by the candidate’s agent.
material_facts: Government employees had given notice that they would strike shortly before the election, and their cooperation was necessary for the election to proceed.
The government considered the employees’ demand for increased allowances legitimate and announced an increase effective at a later date.
The chief minister announced the increase at election meetings.
The evidence did not establish that the government or the chief minister acted as the candidate’s agent.
issues.conclusion: The charge of corrupt practice under section 123(1)(A) was not established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 123(1)(A) concerns a candidate’s or agent’s gift, offer, or promise of gratification to induce electoral support. The allowance increase, announced to meet what the government regarded as a legitimate employee demand, was not a gift, offer, or promise of gratification within that provision; nor was the government or chief minister shown to be the candidate’s agent. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: election_petition_challenging_election and government_increases_employee_benefits and employees_threaten_work_stoppage and government_responds_to_employee_demand and government_not_candidate_agent

predicates.election_petition_challenging_election: A petitioner seeks to set aside an election by alleging a corrupt practice.
predicates.government_increases_employee_benefits: The government announces an increase in benefits for its employees.
predicates.employees_threaten_work_stoppage: Employees threaten to stop work shortly before the election.
predicates.government_responds_to_employee_demand: The government announces the benefit increase in response to a demand it considers legitimate.
predicates.government_not_candidate_agent: The evidence does not show that the government acted as the candidate’s agent in deciding or announcing the increase.

issues.definition: When an election challenge concerns an employee benefit increase announced in response to a work stoppage threat and the government is not shown to be the candidate’s agent, the corrupt-practice charge is not established.

issues.legal_issue: Distributing dummy ballot papers that omit an opposing candidate’s election symbol does not establish a corrupt practice based on misleading voters about that candidate’s candidature when the evidence does not show that the papers or related statements conveyed that the candidate had withdrawn.
material_facts: Dummy ballot papers were printed and distributed on behalf of the successful candidate with his name and symbol and the opposing candidate’s name but not the opposing candidate’s symbol.
The papers contravened Election Commission instructions, but the evidence did not establish that they conveyed to voters that the opposing candidate had withdrawn.
The court rejected testimony that the successful candidate or his agents told voters the opposing candidate had withdrawn.

The evidence showed that voters knew both candidates were contesting, that the opposing candidate’s participation had been publicly acknowledged, and that the successful candidate continued vigorous campaigning.
issues.conclusion: The charge of corrupt practice under section 123(4) was not established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 123(4) addresses specified false statements concerning a candidate’s personal character or conduct, or candidature, made to prejudice that candidate’s electoral prospects. Although the dummy papers violated Election Commission instructions, the evidence did not establish that they conveyed a withdrawal or that the alleged withdrawal statements were made. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: election_petition_challenging_election and misleading_election_material_distributed and opposing_candidate_symbol_omitted and withdrawal_impression_not_proved and alleged_withdrawal_statements_not_proved

predicates.election_petition_challenging_election: A petitioner seeks to set aside an election by alleging a corrupt practice.
predicates.misleading_election_material_distributed: Election material is distributed in a form alleged to mislead voters about an opposing candidate’s candidature.
predicates.opposing_candidate_symbol_omitted: The distributed material names an opposing candidate but omits that candidate’s election symbol.
predicates.withdrawal_impression_not_proved: The evidence does not establish that voters understood the material to mean the opposing candidate had withdrawn.
predicates.alleged_withdrawal_statements_not_proved: The evidence does not establish that the candidate or the candidate’s agents told voters that the opposing candidate had withdrawn.

issues.definition: When allegedly misleading election material omits an opponent’s symbol but neither a withdrawal impression nor alleged withdrawal statements are proved, the corrupt-practice charge is not established.

issues.legal_issue: An allegation that a government employee canvassed for a candidate with the candidate’s consent does not establish a corrupt practice when the evidence that the employee canvassed is not accepted.
material_facts: The petitioner alleged that a police officer who was a government employee actively canvassed for the successful candidate with that candidate’s consent.
The officer and the candidate denied the allegation.
The court rejected the testimony offered to prove the alleged canvassing, finding that it did not warrant acceptance.
issues.conclusion: The charge of corrupt practice under section 123(7) was not established.
issues.legal_principle: Section 123(7) concerns a candidate’s obtaining, procuring, or abetting assistance from a person in government service for the furtherance of the candidate’s election prospects. The alleged canvassing was not established on the evidence. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.election_petition_challenging_election: A petitioner seeks to set aside an election by alleging a corrupt practice.
predicates.government_employee_canvassing_alleged: The petitioner alleges that a person in government service canvassed for a candidate.
predicates.evidence_of_canvassing_rejected: The court does not accept the evidence offered to establish that the government employee canvassed for the candidate.

issues.definition: When an election challenge alleges canvassing by a government employee but the evidence of canvassing is rejected, the corrupt-practice charge is not established.
